extracted.intended_audience: Recipients of Federal financial assistance (elementary/secondary schools, postsecondary institutions, state educational agencies, museums, libraries), Title IX coordinators, institutional administrators, and legal counsel implementing Title IX grievance procedures
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and requirements for designing and operating Title IX grievance procedures across recipients of Federal financial assistance, including distinctions for postsecondary students and employees, due process considerations, bias safeguards, administrative flexibility, and emergency response authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Due Process Applied to Various Recipients and the Department
rubrics_metrics.description: Procedures to resolve allegations of sex discrimination must comport with due process; public postsecondary institutions are subject to constitutional due process, while private recipients are not, but Title IX does not require different procedural standards for public and private recipients. The Department will not administer, enforce, or interpret Title IX in a manner that requires a recipient to deny constitutional rights, and nothing in the regulations requires a recipient to restrict constitutional rights. (See discussion and 34 CFR 106.6(d).)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognizes courts have held public postsecondary disciplinary proceedings subject to procedural due process; the final regulations are intended to allow public recipients to meet constitutional due process requirements (notice and opportunity to be heard) while not imposing different procedural standards on private recipients. Changes to impose or require denial of constitutional rights are precluded.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method for Determining What Process Is Due (Mathews balancing)
rubrics_metrics.description: What process is due must be determined contextually rather than by adopting judicial/criminal procedures wholesale; courts apply the Mathews v. Eldridge factors—(A) the private interest affected; (B) the risk of erroneous deprivation through the procedures used; and (C) the governmental interest at stake—to decide what procedural protections are required.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department concludes §§106.45 and 106.46 satisfy the Mathews factors for Title IX grievance contexts. Agencies must weigh how much an additional procedure would improve reliability against the costs (including societal costs such as discouraging reporting and administrative efficiency). Not all situations calling for procedural safeguards require identical procedures; the presence of a procedure in criminal or civil litigation does not automatically mandate its use in administrative grievance settings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identifying Relevant Interests (balancing complainant and respondent interests)
rubrics_metrics.description: Grievance procedures must take into account multiple, sometimes competing private interests—respondents' interests (e.g., reputation, educational/employment interests) and complainants' interests (e.g., remaining enrolled and having discrimination addressed)—as part of the Mathews analysis and in designing procedures to minimize erroneous outcomes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Procedures should protect against wrongful punishment and reputational harms (e.g., regulate disclosure of information), ensure fairness and reliability, and provide supportive measures to parties. The final regulations incorporate specific provisions to promote accurate and reliable outcomes (e.g., equitable treatment, conflict-of-interest protections, objective evidence evaluation, prohibiting determinations before conclusion of procedures) and to regulate privacy and disclosure (see citations to §106.45(b)(1),(2),(6),(b)(5),(7), (f)(4)(iii), and supportive measures provisions §§106.44(f)(1)(ii),(g),106.45(l)(1)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Issues of Bias (anti-bias safeguards)
rubrics_metrics.description: Grievance procedures must not be tainted by bias; persons designated as Title IX Coordinator, investigator, decisionmaker, or informal resolution facilitator must not have a conflict of interest or bias against complainants or respondents generally or an individual party. The regulations require a presumption that the respondent is not responsible until a determination is made and identify bias as a ground for appeal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Requirements include prohibiting conflicts of interest/bias for designated personnel (§106.45(b)(2); §106.46(a); §106.46(k)(4)), presumption of not responsible (§106.45(b)(3)), making bias a basis for appeal (§§106.45(d)(3),106.46(i)(1)(iii)), and appropriate training to prevent biased procedures (§106.8(d)(2)(iii),(3)). The Department emphasizes the disproportionate impact biased procedures may have on respondents from various backgrounds and that the regulations build on prior anti-bias training provisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Administrative Burdens and Recipient Flexibility
rubrics_metrics.description: The regulations seek to balance standardized, predictable grievance procedures with flexibility to account for diversity among recipients and their administrative capacities. Recipients retain discretion on many procedural elements so long as they keep procedures prompt and equitable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Permissible flexibilities include: setting reasonable timeframes for 'reasonably prompt' procedures (§106.45(b)(4)); using in-house employees or contractors as investigators/decisionmakers (§§106.8(a)(2),106.45(b)(2)); using single decisionmaker or panel (§106.45(b)(2)); offering informal resolution (§106.45(k)); determining remedies/sanctions (§106.45(h)(3),(4)); and formulating appeals (§§106.45(i),106.46(i)). The final rule removed prescriptive 2020 requirements (e.g., mandatory written notice in K–12, live hearings, prohibition of single-investigator model) to reduce burden. The Department declined proposals for safe-harbor exemptions and for allowing recipients to adopt wholly bespoke processes; it also clarifies Title IX's coverage extends beyond Clery Act institutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bifurcation of Sex-Based Harassment Complaints Between Students and Employees at Postsecondary Institutions
rubrics_metrics.description: A postsecondary institution must apply §106.45 to any complaint of sex discrimination (including employee-to-employee sex-based harassment), but must apply §106.46 to any sex-based harassment complaint that involves a student party (including student-complainant vs employee-respondent situations).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The distinction rests on differing legal relationships (employees subject to employment law/Title VII and possibly collective bargaining rights; students do not have Title VII protection as students) and on tailoring protections to students' age, maturity, and needs. §106.46 thus provides additional procedural requirements to ensure equitable participation by students; recipients must harmonize Title IX procedures with Title VII and other applicable employment procedures to the extent not inconsistent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ability To Respond to Threats, Promptly Impose Discipline, or Address Sex Discrimination
rubrics_metrics.description: The regulations do not bar prompt action to address threats or serious misconduct; recipients are required to address complaints 'prompt[ly]' and the rules allow emergency removal or administrative leave where appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recipients may remove a respondent on an emergency basis in certain circumstances (§106.44(h)) and may place an employee respondent on administrative leave during grievance proceedings (§106.44(i)). The Department modified 2020 requirements to address concerns about delay and emphasizes that grievance procedures are intended to enable, not impede, appropriate and timely responses while also offering supportive measures and informal resolution options (§106.44(f)(1)(ii),(iv),(g),(k)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Grievance Procedures Should Not Be Quasi-Judicial or Mimic Courts
rubrics_metrics.description: Stakeholders supported removing quasi-judicial or court-like requirements from grievance procedures so processes are accessible to non-attorneys and do not deter complainants; the final regulations establish baseline procedures usable by non-attorneys and streamline certain prior prescriptive features.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department removed or relaxed features from the 2020 amendments that appeared quasi-judicial (e.g., mandatory live hearing, prescriptive written notices, prohibiting single-investigator model) to create a streamlined process aligned with institutional codes of conduct and increase accessibility and fairness for participants. The baseline is intended to produce fair, transparent, and reliable determinations without imposing unnecessarily legalistic processes that might discourage reporting.
